<reason>A razor-thin call. A's strongest structural play was forcing the "which way does the switch face" question and exploiting B's concession that minors are not load-bearing, which dissolved the motion's "even if" tradeoff. But B answered the switch question directly and plausibly (authentication is already default-on across major platforms), and B's late material systematically neutralized A's remaining routes: the cash-out distinction answered the slot-machine parity question honestly, the "identity infrastructure, not a thirty-second toggle" point repriced A's asymmetry, and the closing "claw machine with a twenty-dollar coin pocket" reframe blunted A's post-PIN conversion story by showing the bankroll is bounded by parental authorization. A's residue — odds display and pull-counted caps living inside the game — was real but narrow, and A never cleanly answered why mandates like odds screens are mere "defaults" that a parent can flip off, leaving B's disproportionality framing standing. Both sides argued the motion as written, answered pressure directly with proper A1/A2 format, and avoided fake precision; both had one clipped turn. B's final position was slightly more internally coherent and did more to close A's live routes than vice versa.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The B4/B5 exchange over the bedroom slot machine: A argued the PIN only guards the currency top-up while forty randomized pulls happen behind it, and B countered that the child cannot pull forty-one times without another authentication, reframing the scenario as a bounded claw-machine bankroll — the sharpest and most consequential clash of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
